eyebrow: Local's Guide to Chai Nat · Updated 2026
intro: Chai Nat is a small Chao Phraya plain province about two and a half hours north of Bangkok that packs in far more variety than its size suggests. One day covers wildlife, temple history, retro markets, and riverside sunsets — all without rushing. We've picked the 10 places people actually talk about, from the sprawling open-air bird park and Thailand's first irrigation dam to Luang Pu Suk's temple and the ancient stupas of Sankhaburi.
chips: 🦜 Chai Nat Bird Park — Largest Open-Air Aviary in Asia
🛕 Luang Pu Suk's Temple, Pak Khlong Makham Thao

blocks.html:
Chai Nat is a small province on the Chao Phraya plain, roughly two and a half hours north of Bangkok. Its charm lies in the variety packed into a short distance — you can do nature, temple history, and riverside chilling all in the same trip. Start the morning at Chai Nat Bird Park on the slopes of Khao Tha Phra while the air is still cool and the birds are active, then head into town to pay respects at Wat Thammamun perched above the Chao Phraya. In the afternoon swing by Wat Pak Khlong Makham Thao — home of the revered Luang Pu Suk — then finish at Chao Phraya Dam for a cool breeze and a sunset. If the weekend happens to fall on the first Saturday or Sunday of the month, there's also the Sapphaya Old Police Station Market, a retro riverside night market to walk through. Chai Nat trips work equally well for families, photography enthusiasts, and anyone needing to escape the city for a day.

Many places on this list are genuine provincial landmarks. The standout is Chai Nat Bird Park — a 26-rai open-air walk-through aviary claimed to be the largest in Asia, housing over 100 bird species alongside a water park, egg museum, and Chao Phraya freshwater fish display hall. Wat Pak Khlong Makham Thao is the temple of Luang Pu Suk Kesaro, one of Thailand's most celebrated monk-masters, whose student Prince Chumphon personally painted murals inside the ubosot that are still visible today. Chao Phraya Dam is Thailand's very first irrigation dam, with a long bridge you can walk or cycle across. The old city of Sankhaburi holds square-based stupas in U-Thong–Lopburi style and star-shaped prangs that will delight anyone who loves ancient architecture. Tick them all off and you'll understand why this quiet riverside province keeps drawing people back.

blocks.name: Chai Nat Bird Park
blocks.area: Khao Tha Phra Sub-district, Mueang Chai Nat District
blocks.signature: 26-rai open-air walk-through aviary — the largest in Asia — with over 100 bird species, a space water park, egg museum, and Chao Phraya freshwater fish hall
blocks.priceRange: 60 THB (foreigners 150 THB) · Water park ticketed separately
blocks.descHtml:
When people think of the top Chai Nat attraction, Chai Nat Bird Park comes to mind first. Open since 1983, it has become the province's defining landmark. The star is the 26-rai open-air enclosure — claimed to be the largest of its kind in Asia — where a giant net covers the entire area and over 100 species of birds live in near-natural conditions. You walk right in among peacocks, cranes, hawks, and eagles flying overhead, which makes it especially popular for families who want kids to experience real birds up close rather than through narrow bars.

Beyond the main aviary, the 248-rai grounds hold plenty more to fill a full day. A favourite among reviewers is the Chao Phraya freshwater fish hall, with over 90 freshwater species and a walk-through fish tunnel that children love. The egg museum is genuinely unusual — a collection of bird eggs from many species — and there's also a planetarium, a giant eagle straw sculpture said to be unique in Thailand, and the Space Water Park with slides for cooling off on hot days (ticketed separately but affordable).

Entry is very good value. Thai adults pay 60 THB, children 25 THB; foreign adults 150 THB, children 75 THB. Senior citizens, people with disabilities, and Chai Nat residents enter free. Open daily 08:30–17:00. The grounds are shaded and leafy overall, though some corners look a little dated and a few pools dry up in the dry season — worth knowing going in.

The location is easy to reach, right on Phahon Yothin Road (Highway 1) at the base of Khao Phlong, Khao Tha Phra Sub-district, about 4 km before Chai Nat town. It's a natural road-trip stop. Plan at least half a day, wear comfortable walking shoes, and bring a hat and water — the grounds are wide and you'll walk more than you expect. A solid first stop for a family trip to Chai Nat.
mustOrder: Walk the 26-rai open-air aviary — largest in Asia
Fish tunnel / Chao Phraya freshwater fish display hall
Space Water Park (great for cooling off in hot weather)
Egg museum + giant eagle straw sculpture
blocks.bestFor: Families with children wanting a full day of wildlife

blocks.name: Chao Phraya Dam
blocks.signature: Thailand's first irrigation dam — a long bridge to walk across, great viewpoint for sunrise and sunset, cycling on the dam crest at dawn
blocks.descHtml:
For anyone passing through Chai Nat who wants somewhere relaxed and free, the Chao Phraya Dam in Bang Luang Sub-district, Sapphaya District is the spot locals keep recommending. Its claim to fame is being Thailand's first large-scale irrigation dam, completed in 1957. The concrete structure stretches over 237 metres with 16 floodgates spanning the Chao Phraya River, and a walkway bridge lets you cross to the other bank — a favourite for casual strolls, family outings, or cyclists looking for an open view.

The highlight most visitors mention is the late afternoon: walk the bridge across the dam crest, catch a cool riverside breeze, and watch the sun drop behind the river. Reviewers say midday can be harsh, but arriving around 5 pm gives comfortable walking conditions and the best light. Another popular angle is watching the water rush through the floodgates — during flood season the current is impressively powerful. Early-morning cyclists routinely come to ride the crest and enjoy the fresh air and clear sky.

No entry fee and no worries about budget — free parking, clean restrooms, and a surrounding Rajabhakti Park to stroll through. There are also a fish market and riverside restaurants nearby. The dam is a short drive from Chai Nat town via Sapphaya District, about 6 km in. Access is possible at any hour, but dawn and dusk are the best windows.

One note: cars are not allowed up on the dam crest — park below and walk up. The setting is naturally simple rather than polished as a tourist attraction, and that understated quality is part of the appeal. If you're coming for big activities, you may find it quiet; but for a scenic wind-down, a sunset photo stop, or an early-morning cycle, it delivers easily — and fits perfectly into a two-day Chai Nat itinerary.
mustOrder: Walk the bridge across the dam crest for a riverside breeze
Catch the sunset around 5 pm when the light is softest
Cycle the dam crest at dawn
Watch water rushing through the floodgates (especially during flood season)
blocks.bestFor: Riverside walk and sunset viewing in the evening, or cycling the crest at dawn
blocks.hours: Open 24 hrs daily (dam crest best at dawn and dusk)
blocks.libCredit: Photo by Mr. Peerapong Prasutr / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

blocks.name: Wat Thammamun Worawihan
blocks.signature: Royal monastery on Thammamun hillside above the Chao Phraya — 565 steps to the summit, the revered Luang Pho Thammajak standing Buddha in Chiang Saen–Sukhothai–Ayutthaya mixed style
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Thammamun Worawihan is the royal monastery most closely tied to Chai Nat's identity. It sits on the slope of Thammamun Hill above the Chao Phraya River, a temple believed to have been founded in the Sukhothai era and restored in the Ayutthaya period. It's ideal for merit-seekers, history and temple-art enthusiasts, and families wanting a scenic temple stop on the old Chai Nat–Nakhon Sawan road. The focal image is Luang Pho Thammajak — a standing Buddha in the 'warding off relatives' posture on a lotus base, admired for its elegant blending of early Chiang Saen–Sukhothai and Ayutthaya styles, with a dhamma-wheel motif on the palm that gives the temple its name.

The must-not-miss is the 565-step stairway up the hill behind the temple, which leads to the viharn housing Luang Pho Nak on the summit. At the top, the view sweeps across the Chao Phraya bend and the town of Chai Nat in the distance. Many visitors describe the wind as cool and the atmosphere deeply peaceful. Those who find the full climb difficult can still pay respects to Luang Pho Thammajak and offer items at the base — the lower temple grounds are equally worthwhile.

Another charming side is the riverside market running along the bank below the bridge in front of the temple, where locals sell homemade food and farm produce at low prices. Many reviewers enjoy a bowl of noodles with their legs dangling over the Chao Phraya after visiting the temple — merit and a meal together.

Free entry, no ticket. Open approximately 08:00–18:00 daily. Google rating is around 4.7 from thousands of reviews, reflecting genuine affection from both locals and visitors. If you plan to climb the 565 steps, wear comfortable shoes and carry water — the stairway is exposed and midday heat is intense. Morning or late afternoon visits give cooler walking conditions and better light for photography.
mustOrder: Pay respects to Luang Pho Thammajak — standing Buddha on lotus base
Climb the 565 steps to the hilltop viharn of Luang Pho Nak
Take in the panoramic bend of the Chao Phraya from the summit
Noodles at the riverside market in front of the temple
blocks.bestFor: Merit-making, riverside views, and stopping at the waterside market
blocks.libCredit: Photo by KOSIN SUKHUM / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

blocks.name: Wat Pak Khlong Makham Thao (Luang Pu Suk)
blocks.area: Wat Sing District, Chai Nat Province
blocks.signature: Temple of the revered monk Luang Pu Suk Kesaro — the ubosot houses mural paintings by H.R.H. Prince Chumphon Khet Udomsak (Sadej Tia), Luang Pu Suk's most famous disciple
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Pak Khlong Makham Thao — commonly called 'Luang Pu Suk's temple' — is an ancient riverside wat at the mouth of Makham Thao Canal in Wat Sing District. Almost everyone passing through Chai Nat stops to pay respects here. Its significance rests on being the temple where Phra Khru Wimol Khunakon (Luang Pu Suk Kesaro), one of Thailand's most celebrated amulet-masters, served as abbot — and on being the temple whose abbot taught Prince Chumphon Khet Udomsak (Sadej Tia), a figure of nationwide reverence. If you follow sacred amulets or enjoy temples with compelling histories, this is exactly your kind of place.

The unmissable highlight is the ubosot, inside which Prince Chumphon personally painted the murals as a gift to Luang Pu Suk during the building of the chapel — a rare piece of royal devotional art found nowhere else in Thailand. After visiting the mural chapel, walk to pay respects to the cast image of Luang Pu Suk and the portrait of Prince Chumphon, then pass under the image base for good fortune — a traditional practice here. The old mondop, Luang Pu Suk's original kuti, and the Guan Yin shrine by the river are also well worth visiting. Many visitors come specifically to ask for protection, safety, and business success.

The atmosphere is calm and leafy, less crowded than major temples in the cities, and the Ta Chin riverside location brings a constant cool breeze. Reviewers consistently note the cleanliness, the warmth of the temple staff, and the pleasantness of a morning or late-afternoon visit. Free entry — only donation boxes and amulet rental for those interested.

The temple is about 25 km from Chai Nat town, along Highway 3183 around km 36–37, easy to drive with parking available. Open daily around 08:00–17:00 (the ubosot may close at midday — allow some flexibility). Dress modestly and, if you want to see the full mural interior, time your visit for when the chapel is open.
mustOrder: Pay respects to the cast image of Luang Pu Suk Kesaro
View Prince Chumphon's hand-painted murals inside the ubosot
Venerate the portrait of Prince Chumphon (Sadej Tia)
Visit the Guan Yin shrine by the Ta Chin River
blocks.bestFor: Seeking blessings from a famous monk's temple — best in the morning or late afternoon
blocks.libCredit: Photo by Mr. Peerapong Prasutr / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

blocks.name: Sapphaya Old Police Station Market (Green Dee Market)
blocks.signature: Retro community market in an old timber police station — vendors in period costume, local food, zero-foam zero-single-use-plastic concept, first Sat–Sun of the month only
blocks.descHtml:
The Sapphaya Old Police Station Market — most people call it Green Dee Market — is a retro community market on the Chao Phraya riverside in Sapphaya District. The standout is the old timber police station dating from RE 120 (around 1901), one of the oldest surviving police stations in Thailand and winner of a conservation award from the Association of Siamese Architects in 2018. It now functions as a small community museum displaying old photographs and local stories. If you enjoy old-school street markets with genuine character rather than the same tourist stalls, this is one to save for your itinerary.

The market highlight is the riverside walking street lined with old wooden shophouses for about 300 metres, many vendors dressed in Thai vintage costume, selling local food and rare traditional Thai sweets. One signature item is 'O-liang Hong Khang' — iced coffee named after the old jail cells, a fun nod to the police station theme. Along the way you'll find street art murals for photos and open food stalls. Reviews repeatedly praise how the market still belongs to the local community rather than being staged for tourists, with food starting at just a few dozen baht. It's also Chai Nat's first zero-foam, zero-single-use-plastic market, using banana leaves and bamboo instead.

Free entry — you only pay for what you eat or take home. The market is on the Chao Phraya riverbank in Sapphaya Sub-district, a short drive from Chai Nat town. The key detail to remember: Green Dee Market opens only on the first Saturday and Sunday of each month, 15:00–21:00 (the old station building and community can be explored in the daytime on weekdays, but stalls are at their liveliest on market days). The market has earned a Thailand Tourism Gold Award in the community tourism category and is widely cited as a model eco-market for secondary cities.

Important: if you specifically want the night market experience, confirm the dates match the first weekend of the month before going — arriving on the wrong day means a very quiet neighbourhood. Bring a cloth bag or tiffin carrier to fit the zero-plastic theme, and keep cash ready as most stalls are cash-only.
mustOrder: O-liang Hong Khang — the market's signature iced coffee
Traditional Thai sweets from local community vendors
Photos in front of the RE 120 timber police station + riverside street art
Walk the old wooden houses along the Chao Phraya
blocks.bestFor: Retro market walkers and local food lovers — come on the first Sat–Sun of the month

blocks.title: 🛏️ Hotels in Chai Nat
blocks.text: If you'd rather not drive back after a full day, staying overnight in Chai Nat town or by the Chao Phraya makes the itinerary much more relaxed. There are small hotels, riverside resorts, and guesthouses at friendly prices. Book ahead through an app to get a better rate and pick the room with the best view.

blocks.name: Chai Nat Muni National Museum
blocks.area: Chai Nat Sub-district, Mueang Chai Nat District
blocks.signature: Two-storey Thai-style museum with prehistoric–Dvaravati artefacts, Buddha images, and ceramics spanning Lopburi, Sukhothai, Ayutthaya, and Rattanakosin periods
blocks.descHtml:
If you enjoy quiet browsing through old artefacts at your own pace, the Chai Nat Muni National Museum is well worth a stop. It sits within the grounds of Wat Phra Borommathat Worawihan — so you can visit the temple first and step straight into the museum. The collection began with Phra Chai Nat Muni, a former provincial head monk who steadily gathered artefacts found in Chai Nat and nearby areas, and it is now curated by the Fine Arts Department. A good choice for anyone wanting to understand the deep roots of this Chao Phraya plain city, or for families looking to give children some historical context.

The two-storey Thai-contemporary building tells the story from prehistoric times upward — stone axes and tools, then Buddha images and ceramics in Lopburi, Sukhothai, Ayutthaya, and Rattanakosin styles. The upper floor holds the most praised items: a collection of historic amulet moulds from different eras, and a gilt bronze Buddha in the Mara-subduing posture described by multiple sources as a rare find. Reviewers like how the collection is manageable — not so vast that you exhaust yourself — and each piece has enough context to make it interesting. A comfortable one-hour walk-through.

Cool, quiet, and never crowded inside. Entry for Thais is 10 THB and foreigners 80 THB — students in uniform and monks enter free, which makes it exceptional value. Open Wednesday to Sunday 09:00–16:00; closed Monday–Tuesday and public holidays. Google rating around 4.3 with visitors praising the helpful, knowledgeable staff.

Since the museum is right next to Wat Phra Borommathat, combine the two in one visit — pay respects at the stupa and then walk into the museum. Parking is available. Because it closes Monday–Tuesday, check the day before you leave to avoid a wasted trip.
mustOrder: Gilt bronze Mara-subduing Buddha — the headline piece on the upper floor
Historic amulet moulds from multiple eras
Prehistoric–Dvaravati artefacts on the ground floor
Lopburi / Sukhothai / Ayutthaya Buddha images and ceramics
blocks.bestFor: History and artefact enthusiasts — pair with a visit to Wat Phra Borommathat

blocks.name: Wat Phra Kaew Sankhaburi
blocks.area: Sankhaburi District (Phraek Si Racha Sub-district), Chai Nat
blocks.signature: Ancient square-based stupa in U-Thong–Lopburi art, fine stucco work, and red sandstone Buddha images with traces of old Khmer artistic influence
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Phra Kaew Sankhaburi is an ancient temple in the old city zone of Phraek Si Racha, about 23 km from Chai Nat town. It's a natural choice for visitors interested in history and ancient architecture. The centrepiece is a tall square-based stupa that many describe as the 'Queen of Stupas in Southeast Asia' — a Lavo-style chedi with U-Thong–late Dvaravati detailing, its tiered square base stepping progressively inward and upward. Niches on all four sides of each tier hold stucco standing Buddha images in the 'bestowing blessings' posture, and the craftsmanship shows a clear mixture of Sukhothai and early Ayutthaya influences — about 600–700 years old.

A second must-see is the Luang Pho Chai viharn in front of the stupa, which houses an ancient red sandstone Buddha. What visitors notice most is the Khmer lintel carved into the wall behind the image, unusually placed face-up rather than face-down as lintels usually are — believed to have been moved here from a nearby ancient Khmer prasat. The grounds also hold the base and red sandstone boundary stones of an old ubosot, offering plenty of fine stonework details for those who enjoy exploring them closely.

The temple grounds are quiet, shaded, and rarely crowded. Multiple genuine reviews describe it as 'ancient, peaceful, worthy of preservation, beautifully atmospheric' and 'ideal for exploring heritage in detail.' Popular with architectural photographers and dedicated temple visitors. Open daily 06:00–18:00; free entry. Morning and evening light is softest for photographing the stupa.

Note: the temple is part of Sankhaburi's cluster of ancient temples — including Wat Mahathat Mueang Sank nearby — so a combined same-day trip is easy. The location is out of town, so a car is most practical. Dress modestly when entering the viharn and allow time to walk the stupa perimeter, because the craftsmanship details reward a slow look.
mustOrder: Square-based stupa — 'Queen of Stupas in Southeast Asia' in U-Thong–Lavo style
Luang Pho Chai red sandstone Buddha + carved Khmer lintel placed face-up behind the image
Stucco standing Buddha images in niches on all four sides of the stupa
Red sandstone boundary stones around the old ubosot base
blocks.bestFor: History and architecture enthusiasts — temple visit and stupa photography at dawn or dusk
blocks.libCredit: Photo by KOSIN SUKHUM / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

blocks.name: Bueng Krachap Yai (Island in the Wetland)
blocks.signature: A wide freshwater wetland with a floating pontoon walkway crossing to the central island — birdwatching, lotus flowers, and golden sunsets
blocks.descHtml:
Bueng Krachap Yai is the largest freshwater wetland in Chai Nat Province — about 1,116 rai of water — located roughly 2 km west of Han Kha District centre. In the middle of the wetland stands 'Ko Mueang Thao U Thong', an island of about 120 rai. The star feature is a pontoon walkway made of bamboo floats that carries you across the water surface to the island — a naturally scenic slow-travel experience for those who value quiet countryside water views over Instagram-staged check-in spots. This is a place to walk slowly, breathe fresh air, and take your time rather than tick it as a quick stop.

What draws people back is the floating walkway itself — surrounded by open water as far as you can see, with lotus flowers blooming in patches and water birds including ducks and open-billed storks living here in numbers. Cyclists can rent bikes for about 20 THB each and pedal leisurely around the island, watching local village life. Those after the best photographs should come in the afternoon as the sun drops — a gentle breeze blows all day, and the late light turns the water surface golden. That moment draws the most praise from visitors.

Free entry, open around 08:30–19:00. The only cost is a bicycle rental if you want to cycle. Fresh-fish restaurants are dotted around the wetland edge. Easy to drive to from Han Kha District town. The site regularly hosts the district's Loy Krathong festival and is a consistent draw for Chai Nat cyclists and nature walkers year-round.

Good to know: this is a simple natural setting — amenities are basic and the experience is about calm rather than activities. The pontoon walkway sways gently as you step, so young children and elderly visitors should take care. Morning or late afternoon visits mean cooler walking and more active birdlife compared with midday.
mustOrder: Walk the bamboo pontoon walkway across the wetland to Ko Mueang Thao U Thong
Rent a bicycle and cycle around the island (~20 THB)
Watch waterbirds, lotus flowers, and the golden sunset from the wetland edge
Fresh fish at a restaurant on the wetland perimeter
blocks.bestFor: Nature lovers after a quiet sunset — best in the late afternoon

blocks.name: Wat Phra Borommathat Worawihan
blocks.area: Chai Nat Sub-district, Mueang Chai Nat District
blocks.signature: Chai Nat's guardian temple — a bell-shaped chedi believed to enshrine Buddha relics
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Phra Borommathat Worawihan is the second-class royal monastery that the people of Chai Nat regard as the province's guardian temple. Its focal feature is a bell-shaped chedi believed to enshrine the Buddha's relics. Anyone drawn to cultural heritage temples, merit-making visits, or the early-Ayutthaya architectural tradition in a quiet setting will appreciate this temple — you get both the blessing of paying respects and a leisurely look at historic craftsmanship in one visit.

Highlights that reviewers consistently mention include the chedi itself — the heart of the temple — followed by the old viharn and ubosot where the original craftsmanship has been preserved, along with important Buddha images inside the viharn that draw regular worshippers. During the annual robe-wrapping ceremony (Hom Pha Phra Borommathat) the temple grounds fill with activity. The Chai Nat Muni National Museum is located right within the temple grounds, so one stop covers both sacred and historical interests.

Free entry and donations as you choose; open daily approximately 06:30–18:00. Location: Chai Nat Sub-district, Mueang Chai Nat District, about 4 km from town along the Chao Phraya. A personal vehicle is most convenient and there is parking inside the temple. From the town centre, a short motorbike taxi ride works if you don't have a car.

Note: this is an active, well-visited temple. Dress modestly — no tank tops or very short shorts — and be mindful of noise near the viharn. The appeal here is the combination of the revered relics, the long history of the temple, and the national museum sharing the same grounds — a single visit satisfies both devotion and curiosity about history.
mustOrder: Pay respects to the bell-shaped Phra Borommathat chedi
Visit the viharn and old ubosot
Step into the Chai Nat Muni National Museum within the grounds
Visit during the annual Hom Pha Phra Borommathat ceremony for the full atmosphere
blocks.bestFor: Temple devotees and cultural visitors — best in the cool morning, or during the annual robe-wrapping ceremony
blocks.libCredit: Photo by KOSIN SUKHUM / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

blocks.name: Wat Mahathat Sankhaburi
blocks.area: Phraek Si Racha Sub-district, Sankhaburi District, Chai Nat Province
blocks.signature: Star-shaped Lopburi-style prangs and an ancient Phra Mahathat base — ancient Buddha images in the old city of Mueang Sank
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Mahathat Sankhaburi is an ancient temple at the heart of the old city of Phraek Si Racha (Mueang Sank), in central Sankhaburi District on the Noi River. Originally called Wat Phra That or Wat Hua Mueang, it predates Ayutthaya and was restored in later eras. The Fine Arts Department designated it a national monument as early as 1935. It suits history travellers, merit-seekers, and photographers looking for quiet heritage shots without the crowds of Ayutthaya — visitors who've been there describe it as a compact version of the Sukhothai Historical Park, much closer to Bangkok.

The unmissable centrepiece is the group of three 'star-shaped prangs' — tall brick-and-mortar towers on square bases in Lopburi-period style. The surface of each prang is deeply ridged in a star or star-fruit cross-section pattern, which is a rare form and the signature style of the Mueang Sank craftsmen. Alongside them is the large red-brick Phra Mahathat base, a cluster of octagonal chedis in U-Thong influence, and the ruins of an old viharn reduced to eight-sided columns and partial walls. Walking the perimeter reveals ancient Buddha images in both Lopburi and early Ayutthaya styles. The main image people come to venerate is Luang Pho Lak Mueang, locally called Luang Pho Mo — often approached with requests for health-related blessings.

Free entry; plan about one to two hours for a comfortable walk-through. Open during daytime hours daily. Morning or late afternoon visits are most pleasant as the monument grounds are fairly open and midday sun is strong. The atmosphere is calm, shaded, and easy to appreciate at a slow pace. The temple is about 20 km from Chai Nat town via Highway 340 to Sankhaburi town, then turning from the district clock tower approximately 500 m.

Worth knowing: this is the centrepiece of the Sankhaburi cluster — Wat Phra Kaew and Wat Song Phi Nong and Wat Totnot Lai are all nearby, making a one-day heritage circuit entirely doable. Dress modestly as this is both a sacred site and a national monument; don't climb on the structures; and if you want the full old-city experience, allow enough time to walk all the way around the prangs and the chedi bases — the craftsmanship detail rewards a careful look.
mustOrder: Three star-shaped prangs — Lopburi-style, the signature of Mueang Sank craftsmen
Large red-brick Phra Mahathat base + octagonal chedis in U-Thong style
Pay respects to Luang Pho Lak Mueang (Luang Pho Mo)
Ancient Buddha images in Lopburi and early Ayutthaya styles
blocks.bestFor: History and temple enthusiasts — quiet old-city heritage walk, best at dawn or late afternoon
blocks.libCredit: Photo by Peetnew / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

blocks.title: Book Tours and Tickets for Chai Nat in Advance
blocks.text: Chai Nat's attractions are spread across several districts. If you'd rather not drive or are coming in a group, guided tours via Klook or GetYourGuide handle routing — some packages include Bangkok pickup and cover several stops in a day. Worth comparing and booking ahead to avoid queues.

blocks.title: Know Before You Go: Chai Nat

items.title: Rent a car or join a tour for the easiest trip
items.text: Attractions spread across several districts with little public transport. Self-driving or hiring a private car from Bangkok is the most convenient option. Grab is scarce even in town — don't depend on it.

items.title: Always bring cash
items.text: Temple offering boxes, the Sapphaya Old Police Station Market, and community food stalls are mostly cash-only. Keep small bills and coins ready; ATMs exist in town but are rare near out-of-town attractions.

items.title: Go early to beat the heat and see the birds active
items.text: The bird park and riverside temples are mostly outdoors. Midday sun is intense — morning visits mean cooler walking and more active birds. Save the Chao Phraya Dam for the evening when the sunset view is best.

items.title: Check dates before heading to the market or museum
items.text: The Sapphaya Old Police Station Market (Green Dee Market) opens only on the first Saturday and Sunday of each month from 15:00–21:00. Chai Nat Muni National Museum is closed Monday and Tuesday. Check before you go.

items.title: Dress modestly for temples
items.text: Chai Nat has many temples and heritage sites. Cover shoulders and knees when entering temple grounds or ubosots, and remove shoes before entering viharns — a courtesy locals take seriously.

items.title: English is limited
items.text: Chai Nat is a secondary city visited mainly by Thais. English signs and menus are scarce. A translation app and temple names saved in Thai script will help a lot — locals are friendly and willing to assist.

blocks.title: Plan Your Chai Nat Day Trip to Cover the Most Ground
blocks.html:
Chai Nat works perfectly as a day trip or a short overnight from Bangkok — the attractions are spread across just a few districts, and routing by zone saves a lot of driving time. Start early at Chai Nat Bird Park on Khao Tha Phra while the air is still cool and the birds are active; let the children explore the open aviary and the water park. Then loop into town to visit the Chai Nat Muni National Museum and Wat Thammamun above the Chao Phraya. Mid-morning, cross to Wat Sing District to visit Wat Pak Khlong Makham Thao, Luang Pu Suk's temple. Afterwards, branch out to the Sankhaburi heritage cluster — Wat Phra Kaew and Wat Mahathat in the ancient city of Phraek Si Racha. Close the day at Chao Phraya Dam on the Sapphaya side, catching the sunset breeze on the dam crest.

Temples and heritage sites are almost all free to enter — donations only. The two paid attractions are Chai Nat Bird Park (Thais 60 THB, foreigners 150 THB; water park extra) and Chai Nat Muni National Museum (Thais 10 THB, foreigners 80 THB). The Sapphaya Old Police Station Market (Green Dee Market) opens only on the first Saturday and Sunday of the month from 15:00–20:00 — work it into the itinerary only if your trip dates line up. Midday heat by the Chao Phraya can be harsh; pack an umbrella, a hat, and a water bottle, and save the dam for the golden hour — it's where most visitors take their best photos.

blocks.text: After exploring several Chai Nat spots, staying overnight beats a late drive back to Bangkok. Check well-located hotels in Chai Nat town and by the Chao Phraya — good value, and booking ahead gets a better room.

faq.q: What are the must-see places in Chai Nat?
faq.a: The two places almost every visitor mentions are Chai Nat Bird Park on Khao Tha Phra — a 26-rai open-air walk-through aviary claimed to be the largest in Asia, with over 100 bird species, a water park, egg museum, and Chao Phraya fish hall — and the Chao Phraya Dam in Sapphaya District, Thailand's first irrigation dam, where you can walk a long bridge and watch the sun set over the river. Both are provincial icons that nearly every Chai Nat trip includes.

faq.q: What else does Chai Nat have beyond the bird park?
faq.a: Beyond the bird park and the Chao Phraya Dam, Chai Nat has strong offerings in the heritage and temple categories. Wat Pak Khlong Makham Thao is the temple of Luang Pu Suk Kesaro, whose student Prince Chumphon personally painted murals inside the ubosot that survive to this day. Wat Thammamun Worawihan sits above the Chao Phraya with 565 steps and a sweeping river view from the summit. The old city of Sankhaburi holds Wat Phra Kaew with its tall square-based Lavo-style stupa and Wat Mahathat with its rare star-shaped Lopburi prangs. The Sapphaya Old Police Station Market (Green Dee Market) is a retro community market open on the first Saturday and Sunday of the month, and Wat Phra Borommathat Worawihan is the province's own guardian temple.

faq.q: Do Chai Nat attractions charge entry?
faq.a: Most temples and heritage sites in the list are free to enter — donations only. These include Wat Thammamun, Wat Pak Khlong Makham Thao, Wat Phra Kaew Sankhaburi, Wat Mahathat Sankhaburi, and Wat Phra Borommathat Worawihan. Chao Phraya Dam and Bueng Krachap Yai wetland are also free. Paid attractions: Chai Nat Bird Park (Thais 60 THB, foreigners 150 THB; water park priced separately) and Chai Nat Muni National Museum (Thais 10 THB, foreigners 80 THB). The Sapphaya Old Police Station Market is free entry with food starting from around 20–60 THB.

faq.q: How to get to Chai Nat and what about parking?
faq.a: The most convenient way is to drive or hire a car from Bangkok — roughly two and a half hours — because attractions are spread across several districts including Mueang Chai Nat, Sapphaya, Wat Sing, Sankhaburi, and Han Kha. Most major sites like Chai Nat Bird Park, Chao Phraya Dam, and the various temples have wide, free parking lots. If you don't have a car, minivans and long-distance buses from Bangkok serve Chai Nat town, and you can then take songthaew or motorcycle taxis to individual sites — though this is considerably less convenient than self-driving given how dispersed the attractions are.

faq.q: What time do Chai Nat attractions open?
faq.a: Temples generally open for worship from early morning to evening every day. Chai Nat Bird Park opens around 08:00–18:00 — go in the morning when the air is cool and the birds are most active. The Sapphaya Old Police Station Market (Green Dee Market) opens only on the first Saturday and Sunday of the month, 15:00–20:00, so check dates before going. Chao Phraya Dam is best at dawn for cycling or in the evening for the sunset. Wat Phra Borommathat Worawihan opens daily around 06:30–18:00. Always check individual opening times before you head out.
